<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the impact of China’s mixed-ownership reform on the innovation of non-state-owned acquirers, with a particular focus on the impact on firms with high financing constraints, low-quality accounting information or less tangible assets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use a proprietary dataset of firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges to investigate the impact of mixed ownership reform on non-state-owned enterprise (non-SOE) innovation. We employ regression analysis to examine the association between mixed ownership reform and firm innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study finds that non-state-owned firms can improve innovation by acquiring equity in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) under the reform. Eased financing constraints, lowered financing costs, better access to tax incentives or government subsidies, lowered agency costs, better accounting information quality and more credit loans are underlying the impact. Additionally, cross-ownership connections amongst non-SOE executives and government intervention strengthen the impact, whilst regional marketisation weakens it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adds to the literature on the association between mixed ownership reform and firm innovation by focussing on the conditions under which this impact is stronger. It also sheds light on the policy implications for SOE reforms in emerging economies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mixed ownership reform and non-state-owned enterprise innovation: Evidence from China

items.abstract: <jats:p> The new state-owned enterprise (SOE) mixed ownership reform have some distinct features that were not addressed in previous reforms. While some central SOEs and local governments have unveiled their own plans to diversify ownership structure, the success of the reform hinges on how the government resolves two credibility problems: one is to restore credibility to the reform commitment and the other is to convince private investors that their interests will be sufficiently protected. </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Abstract: Mixed-ownership reform is a central component of China's high-quality economic transition, while reverse mixed-ownership reform has emerged as a novel paradigm of state–private capital integration. By introducing state-owned capital into the private sector, this reform provides an institutional channel through which private firms could alleviate resource constraints and catalyse strategic transformation. Using data on China's listed private enterprises from 2003 to 2019, this article empirically investigates the impact of reverse mixed-ownership reform on private enterprise growth and its underlying mechanisms. The results demonstrate that reverse mixed-ownership reform significantly promotes private enterprise growth. These findings remain valid and robust after addressing potential endogeneity concerns and conducting a series of robustness checks. Mechanism analysis reveals that the reform drives enterprise growth through three primary channels: reducing institutional costs, expanding access to external financing and strengthening innovation incentives. The positive effect is more pronounced among firms operating in regions with weaker institutional environments, firms facing severe financing constraints and firms operating in low-barrier industries. This article provides both theoretical insights and practical implications for deepening mixed-ownership reform, promoting the high-quality development of the private sector and strengthening national governance systems and capabilities.</jats:p>
title: How State-owned Capital Participation Impacts Private Enterprise Growth? Evidence from the Reverse Mixed-ownership Reform

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study examines a previously unexplored corporate governance mechanism, that is, the presence of central state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) as non‐controlling shareholders in local SOEs in China, and investigates its impact on corporate innovation. Our research reveals that central SOE ownership enhances local SOE innovation. Further analyses based on the 2016 top‐down innovation‐related policy and policy uncertainty provide additional evidence that central SOE ownership serves as a channel for transmitting policy information to local SOEs and improves their innovation. Moreover, we show that central SOE ownership and private ownership function as complements in fostering innovation of local SOEs. The positive effect of central SOE ownership, however, is attenuated by stronger local government intervention and greater geographic distance between local and central SOEs. Overall, our findings highlight the governance role of central SOE ownership, attributable to its higher hierarchical position within the political system. By illuminating the role of shareholder identity and political hierarchy, this study contributes to the literature on non‐controlling shareholders and extends research on the heterogeneity of state ownership, thereby offering important implications for SOE governance.</jats:p>
title: Central State‐Owned Enterprise Ownership and Local State‐Owned Enterprise Innovation: Evidence From China
